Petrini, who has served as Vice Governor since 2021, steps into the position following recent legal reforms enacted by Pope Francis. These changes, which modify the Fundamental Law of Vatican City (May 13, 2023) and Law No. CCLXXIV on the Government of the Vatican City State (November 25, 2018), remove the requirement that the governorship be held exclusively by a cardinal. Additionally, the revisions introduce a new structural adjustment—where there will now be two vice governors instead of one.
On February 25, the Vatican announced the appointment of these two new vice governors. Monsignor Emilio Nappa, previously Adjunct Secretary of the Dicastery for Evangelization and President of the Pontifical Mission Societies, will bring his ecclesiastical expertise to the role. Meanwhile, Giuseppe Puglisi-Alibrandi, who has served as Deputy Secretary General of the Vatican’s Governatorate, will contribute his extensive administrative experience. This means that, for the first time, the Vatican’s government will be led by a woman, supported by both a cleric and a layman.
Beyond simply holding the title, Sister Raffaella Petrini has been granted the authority to delegate specific responsibilities and assignments to the two vice governors. This reflects the Pope’s trust in her leadership and decision-making, reinforcing his broader efforts to elevate the role of women in Vatican administration.
While the Vatican remains deeply rooted in tradition, Pope Francis continues to open doors for women in key leadership positions, a move that is likely to shape the future of the Church’s institutional framework.

POPE APPOINTS SISTER RAFAELLA PETRINI AS PRESIDENT OF PONTIFICAL COMMISSION AND GOVERNORATE OF VATICAN CITY STATE
Another woman takes over a top job at the Vatican, this time running the city state administration.
Pope Francis has appointed Sister Raffaella Petrini as the new President of the Pontifical Commission for Vatican City State and President of the Governorate of Vatican City State.
A statement released by the Holy See Press Office on Saturday also said the appointment is effective March 1, 2025.
With this appointment, she becomes the first woman to hold the highest leadership position within the Vatican’s administrative structure.
In her new role, she will oversee the governance of Vatican City, managing its daily operations and policies in accordance with the directives of the Holy See. The Governorate is responsible for various aspects of Vatican City's administration, including security, infrastructure, and cultural heritage.
Sister Petrini’s predecessor, Cardinal Fernando Vérgez Alzaga, L.C., served as President since 2021.
Last month, Francis named the first woman to head a major Holy See office, appointing another Italian nun, Sister Simona Brambilla, to become prefect of the department responsible for all the Catholic Church’s religious orders.

The post of **Governor of the Vatican City State** (Italian: _Governatore dello Stato della Città del Vaticano_) was held by Marchese Camillo Serafini from the foundation of the state in 1929 until his death in 1952. The governor had power to appoint and supervise the people running the city state. During Serafini's lifetime, the powers of the governor were limited by Pope Pius XII in 1939 by the establishment of the Pontifical Commission for Vatican City State. No successor was appointed and the position was abolished on Serafini's death.
The Pontifical Commission for Vatican City State has exercised the functions that were previously attributed to the governor since 1952. The President of the commission has also held the title of President of the Governorate of the Vatican City State since 2001, which has the responsibilities of the governor of the state.
texts.1: After the rise of Fascist Italy, there was a drive to introduce a _governo_ (governor) to take responsibility for running the remaining Papal estate, which, following the unification of Italy, was limited to the Leonine City in Rome.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Vatican_City#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGentile2024108-1) The term _governo_ was used as the person was the "govern" the city, but their responsibility was similar to a mayor.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Vatican_City#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGentile2024109-2) The first person to be appointed to the role was Marchese Camillo Serafini, who took office at the creation of the Vatican City on 11 February 1929.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Vatican_City#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPavelli1959134-3) On 20 March 1939, Pope Pius XII created the Pontifical Commission for Vatican City State, which had representation from the laity as well as cardinals.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Vatican_City#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilliamsKernan19588-4) The role of the commission was to present the pope's positions and ensure governance of the state aligned with papal policy.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Vatican_City#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGentile202439-5) Pius XII placed the commission over the governor and so limited the powers of the office.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Vatican_City#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGentile2024138-6) Over time,

many of the governor's responsibilities were passed to a Special Delegate that was appointed by the Pontifical Commission for Vatican City State on the advice of the pope.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Vatican_City#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGentile2024179-7) Serafini remained in post as governor until his death on 21 March 1952.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Vatican_City#cite_note-Time-8)
Serafini was not replaced and the role was taken over by the Pontifical Commission for Vatican City State which consisted of two cardinals and two members of the laity, fulfilling one of Pope Pius XII's dreams that the Vatican City would be ruled by collegiate governance.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Vatican_City#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGentile2024116-9)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Vatican_City#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWilliamsKernan19588-4) However, this produced a political problem with executive power uncertain, which subsequent popes attempted to address throughout the remainder of the century.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Vatican_City#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGentile2024181-10) In July 1969, the roles of Special Delegate, president of the Council of State and president of the Pontifical Commission for Vatican City State were combined.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Vatican_City#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBull198251%E2%80%9352-11) This was further reformed by Pope John Paul II in the Fundamental Law of Vatican City State of 26 November 2000 with the introduction of the title of President of the Governorate of the Vatican City State,

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
The **politics of Vatican City** take place in a framework of a theocraticabsoluteelective monarchy, in which the Pope, religiously speaking, the leader of the Catholic Church and Bishop of Rome, exercises _ex officio_ supreme legislative, executive, and judicial power over the Vatican City as it is being governed by the Holy See,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics_of_Vatican_City#cite_note-1) a rare case of non-hereditary monarchy.
The term "Holy See" refers to the composite of the authority, jurisdiction, and sovereignty vested in the Pope and his advisers to direct the worldwide Catholic Church. It is therefore quite distinct from the Vatican City state, which was created in 1929, through the Lateran treaties between the Holy See and Italy.
As the "central government" of the Catholic Church, the Holy See has a legal personality that allows it to enter into treaties as the juridical equal of a state and to send and receive diplomatic representatives. It has formal diplomatic relations with 179 nations.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics_of_Vatican_City#cite_note-2) The State of Vatican City, for its part, is recognized under international law as a sovereign territory. Unlike the Holy See, it does not receive or send diplomatic representatives, and the Holy See acts on its behalf in international affairs.
The pope is elected in the papal conclave, composed of all the cardinal electors which are bishops and archbishops appointed by the pope, now limited to all the cardinals below the age of 80, after the death or resignation of the previous Pope. The Conclave is held in the Sistine Chapel, where all the electors are locked in (Latin: _cum clave_) until the election for which a two-thirds majority is required. The faithful can follow the results of the polls, usually two in the morning and two in the evening, until election, by a chimney-top, visible from [St. Peter's Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Peter's_Square "St. Peter's Square"). The voting papers are burnt in a stove attached to the chimney. Additives make the smoke black (_fumata nera_) in a case of no election, or white (_fumata bianca_) when the new pope is elected.
texts.1: The Dean of the Sacred College (_Cardinale Decano_) will then ask the freshly elected pope to choose his pastoral name. As soon as the pope is dressed with the white cassock, the Senior Cardinal-Deacon (_Cardinale Protodiacono_) appears on the major balcony of St. Peter's façade to introduce the new pope,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics_of_Vatican_City#cite_note-3) with the Latin sentence _Annuntio vobis gaudium magnum: habemus papam_ (I announce to you a great joy: We have a Pope).

## Administration of Vatican City
[edit]
The flag of Vatican City
As with almost all monarchies, the executive, legislative and judicial power of government reside in the crown, in this case in the office of the Bishop of Rome (the pope). As with many monarchies, the pope exercises this power through other organs which act on his behalf and in his name.
The pope commonly delegates the internal administration of Vatican City to various bodies and officials. However, according to the Fundamental Law of Vatican City State, "The Supreme Pontiff, sovereign of Vatican City State, has the fullness of legislative, executive, and judicial powers"[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics_of_Vatican_City#cite_note-4) for Vatican City.
The pope delegates legislative authority for the state to the unicameralPontifical Commission for Vatican City State. This commission was established in 1939 by Pope Pius XII. It consists of seven Cardinals appointed by the pope for five-year terms. Laws passed by the Commission must be approved by the pope through the Secretariat of State prior to being published and taking effect.
The President of the Pontifical Commission is also the President of the Governorate of Vatican City, to whom the pope delegates executive authority for the state. The president is assisted by a Secretary General and a Vice Secretary General. Each of these officers is appointed by the pope for a five-year term. Actions of the President must be approved by the commission. Various departments and offices report to the Governorate, handling such issues as communications, internal security, fire protection, and the Vatican Museums. The Corpo della Gendarmeria is the state's security and police force, not the Pontifical Swiss Guard, which is an organ of the Holy See, not of Vatican City.

## Administration of Vatican City
The Pope is _ex officio_sovereign and head of state of the Vatican City State since 1929. He delegates executive authority to the President of the Pontifical Commission for Vatican City State, who is _ex officio_ President of the Governorate and _de facto_head of government of Vatican. The president is appointed by the Pope for a five-year term, but may be removed at any time by the pope.
The president reports all important matters to the Secretariat of State, the Pope's chief everyday advisory body, which is consulted on all matters, even if they belong to the specific competence of the Commission for Vatican City State or, for instance, that of the Congregation for Catholic Education. The Secretariat of State is not thereby considered to hold responsibility for such matters, and the Cardinal Secretary of State is not seen as heading the Vatican City State or the various departments of the Roman Curia, other than the Secretariat of State itself.
Vatican City is a member of CEPT, Eutelsat, International Grains Council, Intelsat, ITU and UPU.
Vatican City does not have direct diplomatic relations with other states. Its foreign relations are managed by the Holy See. See Holy See – Relationship with the Vatican City and other territories.
A unicameral Pontifical Commission for Vatican City State, appointed by the Pope, operates as legislative branch, proposing law and policy to the Pope.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics_of_Vatican_City#cite_note-5) Prior to taking effect, laws and policies passed by the commission must be approved by the Supreme Pontiff, through the Secretariat of State,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics_of_Vatican_City#cite_note-6) and be published in the Italian-language supplement of the _Acta Apostolicae Sedis_ that deals with Vatican City State matters.
The "Councillors of the State" give their consultation in the drafting of legislation.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics_of_Vatican_City#cite_note-7) They may be consulted either alone or collegially.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics_of_Vatican_City#cite_note-8)
The seal of Vatican City State

## Administration of Vatican City
As a sovereign state, Vatican City has a legal system distinct from that of Italy. The pope's judicial authority is exercised through the Prefect of the Supreme Tribunal of the Apostolic Signatura, as he by law serves also as the President of the Cassation Court of Vatican City (i.e. the highest court of appeal).[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics_of_Vatican_City#cite_note-9)
The population of the state is a few hundred. Each day outsiders come there to work. 18 million people visit there each year.
In one year its courts tried 640 civil cases and 226 penal cases.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics_of_Vatican_City#cite_note-10)

In memory of Phil Serafini--
Born in Boulder, Colorado to Philip George Serafini, Jr. and Ruth Harris Lockett, he lived his early years in Denver, Colorado with younger sisters Lynn (Serafini) Seaman and Frosty Lee Serafini. He would often tell stories of his biking adventures along Sand Creek and visits to the Museum of Nature and Science, which remained his favorite museum throughout his life (dragging his subsequent children and grandchildren through it many times). He spent his summers on long road trips where he day-dreamed about being a cowboy and travelled to visit his mom’s family in Pratt, Kansas where he got his first taste for farm life. He loved the outdoors, science, and sports. He also had a knack for numbers and reveled in his dad challenging him with increasingly difficult mental-math problems, which would come in handy later on. He graduated from George Washington high school where he wrestled and played football (’65).
He then attended Knox College (’69) in Galesburg, IL, a place that would help set the trajectory of his life. At Knox, he played football, wrestled, was a member of the Tau Kappa Epsilon fraternity, and majored in political science. He made many friends at Knox whose friendships truly lasted a lifetime. At Knox, he met his beautiful, talented, and brilliant wife Mary Alice (Schenker) Serafini. She would become the person with whom he would circumnavigate the world, build a family, and do life with for decades to come. Upon graduation, they married on April 5, 1969, in Mary Alice’s hometown, Bloomington, Illinois.
After graduation, they set out on the greatest adventures of their lives. Perhaps heeding John F. Kennedy’s call to public service, or possibly trying to avoid Phil getting drafted for the Vietnam War, Phil and Mary Alice enlisted in the Peace Corps where they served in Sierra Leone from 1969-1972, Phil working with farmers in rice paddy development and Mary Alice teaching English. Phil found his life’s calling then--on the farm and overseas--and made life-long friends.

With their Peace Corps service complete, Phil and Mary Alice travelled throughout Africa and Europe, before settling in France for a brief stay where Mary Alice taught English and Phil made his first attempts at speaking French. Phil being Phil, also managed to finagle a job where he would help French businessmen practice their English over nice meals. They eventually made their way to America’s breadbasket, Sacramento, California, to further their education at UC Davis. Phil earned his Masters in Agronomy. They got their first of many dogs, Tache, a dalmatian, who accompanied Phil for many hours of fieldwork. California suited them nicely but the pull of West Africa and adventure was strong.
In 1978, Phil accepted a job with the International Crops Research Institute for the Semi-arid Tropics (ICRISAT). He and Mary Alice moved to Bamako, Mali and then later to Niamey, Niger where Phil managed research farms. During the span of those years, they would welcome their three children into the world -- Juliana, Ted, and Timothy -- and forged bonds with other families that still remain.
Phil built a life for himself in Mali and then Niger that any kid who dreamed of being a cowboy would be jealous of. On the farm, Phil worked with colleagues that became some of his closest friends. He got a thrill out of installing new irrigation equipment and racing his friend Mick O’Neill on horseback. The Serafini’s and their close friends would spend weekends camping at the farm. The parents would put the kids on horses and let them ride by themselves for hours. All survived, although not without a close call or two.
At home, he filled the yard with animals you might find anywhere--dogs, chickens, ducks, rabbits, and a horse. But (to his children’s great delight) he also added a tortoise big enough for a car axle to get stuck on (a common occurrence), a peacock, and he often arrived home from the farm with animals that were probably best left in nature--a monitor lizard, an African gray parrot, owl, and serval cat, to name a few. All but the monitor lizard were released back into the wild. The lizard escaped into the yard with the help of Tim and a few friends (that’s a story for another day). Phil and Mary Alice also took their kids on countless adventures, including several safaris where they escaped getting trampled by elephants on more than one occasion.

As the kids grew older, Phil and Mary Alice decided it was time to move back to the U.S. In 1990, they moved to Fayetteville, Arkansas, where Phil had accepted a job with the University of Arkansas. The natural beauty of Arkansas was a perfect place for Phil to help cultivate in his kids a love for the outdoors and nature. Life-long family friends from their time in Africa, Shad and Linda Okiror and sons, eventually also moved nearby. Phil spent many summers taking his kids, the Okiror boys, and other kids canoeing on the Buffalo and King Rivers, fishing nearby lakes, and catching the local critters--snapping turtles, crawdaddies, banded water snakes and more.
His time at the University of Arkansas helped set the stage for the next great adventure in his life. While there, he had the opportunity to travel to Bolivia where he fell in love with the generous people, lively culture, and the country’s natural beauty. He helped start a program for Bolivian students to attend the University of Arkansas to complete their bachelors, masters, and doctoral degrees. He eventually left the U of A to focus on agricultural ventures in Santa Cruz, Bolivia. For the next twenty years, he commuted from Fayetteville to Bolivia where Phil lived a fulfilling life growing soybeans and chia seeds, managing a cattle ranch, and expanding his expertise in insect control and irrigation. In addition to devoting himself to farming, he connected with people. As he had elsewhere, his professional relationships morphed into meaningful friendships. He helped mentor the young and build relationships with the local community.
Phil loved being a dad, uncle, grandfather, father-figure, and mentor to many. As a dad, Phil was a believer that education did not just happen in the classroom. There were forests, creeks, and ponds to explore. And sports were where you could find community, develop mental toughness, and learn how to overcome challenges. In the classroom and out, he would push his kids to challenge themselves and let them know he believed in them even if others didn’t or they didn’t believe themselves. He didn’t do this type of mentoring just for his kids. He had a way of helping, prodding, pushing, and giving someone just enough confidence to take on a big challenge.
After a long international career, he decided to settle back in Fayetteville, AR in his later years. He never stopped his pursuit of agricultural learning and endeavors.

Throughout all his personal and professional experiences and achievements, he developed lasting friendships.
No longer able to thrive in living life, Phil passed away peacefully on Friday, August 21, 2026, at Circle of Life in Springdale, AR. He was preceded in death by Philip George Serafini Jr., Ruth Harris Lockett, and Frosty Lee Serafini. He is survived by his wife of 57 years, Mary Alice (Schlenker) Serafini, daughter, Juliana Serafini Kelty (Josef), sons Ted Philip Serafini (Ellen) and Timothy Tavenner Serafini. His grandchildren include Dayton Marie Sewald, Kendall Alice Kelty, Paul Felix Serafini and Max Philip Serafini. His sister Lynn Serafini Seaman (Tom) and family, sister-in-law Marty Graner (Bill) and brother-in-law Henry Schlenker (Gayle) and families.
In lieu of flowers, the family asks you consider planting a garden (or backyard farm), starting a compost pile, or donating to an organization of your choice.
A celebration of Phil’s life will be held at a later date.

Church of San Francesco, Mantua  
In Mantua, the Gonzaga family marked their rapid ascent to prominence by commissioning in the church of San Francesco a large funerary chapel. The church was largely destroyed during World War II but fortunately the Gonzaga chapel survived.
The Gonzaga chapel is the largest of the church's noble chapels, occupying the most prestigious location close to the apse. Here the bodies of princes and their consorts reposed in marble tombs - now largely removed - among brilliantly coloured frescoes that covered the chapel's vault and walls. Although only partially preserved, these paintings still give an idea of the extravagant visions of both patron and painter in realizing this commission. The artist, who illustrated scenes from the lives of Christ and St Louis of Toulouse, was the Modenese painter Serafino Serafini, a pupil of the more famous Tommaso da Modena.

# Death of St Louis by SERAFINI, Serafino
### Death of St Louis
after 1375
Fresco
Church of San Francesco, Mantua  
In Mantua, the Gonzaga family marked their rapid ascent to prominence by commissioning in the church of San Francesco a large funerary chapel. The church was largely destroyed during World War II but fortunately the Gonzaga chapel survived.
The Gonzaga chapel is the largest of the church's noble chapels, occupying the most prestigious location close to the apse. Here the bodies of princes and their consorts reposed in marble tombs - now largely removed - among brilliantly coloured frescoes that covered the chapel's vault and walls. Although only partially preserved, these paintings still give an idea of the extravagant visions of both patron and painter in realizing this commission. The artist, who illustrated scenes from the lives of Christ and St Louis of Toulouse, was the Modenese painter Serafino Serafini, a pupil of the more famous Tommaso da Modena.

In memory of Phil Serafini--
Born in Boulder, Colorado to Philip George Serafini, Jr. and Ruth Harris Lockett, he lived his early years in Denver, Colorado with younger sisters Lynn (Serafini) Seaman and Frosty Lee Serafini. He would often tell stories of his biking adventures along Sand Creek and visits to the Museum of Nature and Science, which remained his favorite museum throughout his life (dragging his subsequent children and grandchildren through it many times). He spent his summers on long road trips where he day-dreamed about being a cowboy and travelled to visit his mom’s family in Pratt, Kansas where he got his first taste for farm life. He loved the outdoors, science, and sports. He also had a knack for numbers and reveled in his dad challenging him with increasingly difficult mental-math problems, which would come in handy later on. He graduated from George Washington high school where he wrestled and played football (’65).
He then attended Knox College (’69) in Galesburg, IL, a place that would help set the trajectory of his life. At Knox, he played football, wrestled, was a member of the Tau Kappa Epsilon fraternity, and majored in political science. He made many friends at Knox whose friendships truly lasted a lifetime. At Knox, he met his beautiful, talented, and brilliant wife Mary Alice (Schenker) Serafini. She would become the person with whom he would circumnavigate the world, build a family, and do life with for decades to come. Upon graduation, they married on April 5, 1969, in Mary Alice’s hometown, Bloomington, Illinois.
After graduation, they set out on the greatest adventures of their lives. Perhaps heeding John F. Kennedy’s call to public service, or possibly trying to avoid Phil getting drafted for the Vietnam War, Phil and Mary Alice enlisted in the Peace Corps where they served in Sierra Leone from 1969-1972, Phil working with farmers in rice paddy development and Mary Alice teaching English. Phil found his life’s calling then--on the farm and overseas--and made life-long friends.
texts.1:
With their Peace Corps service complete, Phil and Mary Alice travelled throughout Africa and Europe, before settling in France for a brief stay where Mary Alice taught English and Phil made his first attempts at speaking French. Phil being Phil, also managed to finagle a job where he would help French businessmen practice their English over nice meals. They eventually made their way to America’s breadbasket, Sacramento, California, to further their education at UC Davis. Phil earned his Masters in Agronomy. They got their first of many dogs, Tache, a dalmatian, who accompanied Phil for many hours of fieldwork. California suited them nicely but the pull of West Africa and adventure was strong.
In 1978, Phil accepted a job with the International Crops Research Institute for the Semi-arid Tropics (ICRISAT). He and Mary Alice moved to Bamako, Mali and then later to Niamey, Niger where Phil managed research farms. During the span of those years, they would welcome their three children into the world -- Juliana, Ted, and Timothy -- and forged bonds with other families that still remain.
Phil built a life for himself in Mali and then Niger that any kid who dreamed of being a cowboy would be jealous of. On the farm, Phil worked with colleagues that became some of his closest friends. He got a thrill out of installing new irrigation equipment and racing his friend Mick O’Neill on horseback. The Serafini’s and their close friends would spend weekends camping at the farm. The parents would put the kids on horses and let them ride by themselves for hours. All survived, although not without a close call or two.
At home, he filled the yard with animals you might find anywhere--dogs, chickens, ducks, rabbits, and a horse. But (to his children’s great delight) he also added a tortoise big enough for a car axle to get stuck on (a common occurrence), a peacock, and he often arrived home from the farm with animals that were probably best left in nature--a monitor lizard, an African gray parrot, owl, and serval cat, to name a few. All but the monitor lizard were released back into the wild. The lizard escaped into the yard with the help of Tim and a few friends (that’s a story for another day). Phil and Mary Alice also took their kids on countless adventures, including several safaris where they escaped getting trampled by elephants on more than one occasion.
texts.2:
As the kids grew older, Phil and Mary Alice decided it was time to move back to the U.S. In 1990, they moved to Fayetteville, Arkansas, where Phil had accepted a job with the University of Arkansas. The natural beauty of Arkansas was a perfect place for Phil to help cultivate in his kids a love for the outdoors and nature. Life-long family friends from their time in Africa, Shad and Linda Okiror and sons, eventually also moved nearby. Phil spent many summers taking his kids, the Okiror boys, and other kids canoeing on the Buffalo and King Rivers, fishing nearby lakes, and catching the local critters--snapping turtles, crawdaddies, banded water snakes and more.
His time at the University of Arkansas helped set the stage for the next great adventure in his life. While there, he had the opportunity to travel to Bolivia where he fell in love with the generous people, lively culture, and the country’s natural beauty. He helped start a program for Bolivian students to attend the University of Arkansas to complete their bachelors, masters, and doctoral degrees. He eventually left the U of A to focus on agricultural ventures in Santa Cruz, Bolivia. For the next twenty years, he commuted from Fayetteville to Bolivia where Phil lived a fulfilling life growing soybeans and chia seeds, managing a cattle ranch, and expanding his expertise in insect control and irrigation. In addition to devoting himself to farming, he connected with people. As he had elsewhere, his professional relationships morphed into meaningful friendships. He helped mentor the young and build relationships with the local community.
Phil loved being a dad, uncle, grandfather, father-figure, and mentor to many. As a dad, Phil was a believer that education did not just happen in the classroom. There were forests, creeks, and ponds to explore. And sports were where you could find community, develop mental toughness, and learn how to overcome challenges. In the classroom and out, he would push his kids to challenge themselves and let them know he believed in them even if others didn’t or they didn’t believe themselves. He didn’t do this type of mentoring just for his kids. He had a way of helping, prodding, pushing, and giving someone just enough confidence to take on a big challenge.
After a long international career, he decided to settle back in Fayetteville, AR in his later years. He never stopped his pursuit of agricultural learning and endeavors.
texts.3:
Throughout all his personal and professional experiences and achievements, he developed lasting friendships.
No longer able to thrive in living life, Phil passed away peacefully on Friday, August 21, 2026, at Circle of Life in Springdale, AR. He was preceded in death by Philip George Serafini Jr., Ruth Harris Lockett, and Frosty Lee Serafini. He is survived by his wife of 57 years, Mary Alice (Schlenker) Serafini, daughter, Juliana Serafini Kelty (Josef), sons Ted Philip Serafini (Ellen) and Timothy Tavenner Serafini. His grandchildren include Dayton Marie Sewald, Kendall Alice Kelty, Paul Felix Serafini and Max Philip Serafini. His sister Lynn Serafini Seaman (Tom) and family, sister-in-law Marty Graner (Bill) and brother-in-law Henry Schlenker (Gayle) and families.
In lieu of flowers, the family asks you consider planting a garden (or backyard farm), starting a compost pile, or donating to an organization of your choice.
A celebration of Phil’s life will be held at a later date.
